title: Forces and motion — speed, velocity and acceleration
examTip: Always check whether a question asks for speed (scalar) or velocity (vector). They are different quantities. Mixing them up costs marks.
introTips: Speed and velocity look almost the same. The difference is direction. That one detail matters hugely in physics.
Graphs are worth a lot of marks. Know what gradient and area mean on distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
Equations of motion questions nearly always give you three values and ask for a fourth. Find your u, v, a, s and t before writing anything.
intro: Every road sign, speed camera and sat-nav relies on the physics in this topic. Speed, velocity and acceleration let us describe motion precisely. Being precise is how you pick up every mark in the exam.

basics.text: Distance is measured in metres (m) and time in seconds (s). 1 km is 1000 m.
A graph has two lines called axes. The x-axis runs along the bottom. The y-axis runs up the side. Each axis shows a quantity and its unit.
5² means 5 × 5 = 25. The square root of 25 is 5, because 5 × 5 = 25.

keyPoints.heading: Scalar and vector quantities
keyPoints.content: Physics quantities are split into two types. Scalar quantities have magnitude (size) only. There is no direction attached. Examples include distance, speed, mass, energy and temperature. Vector quantities have both magnitude AND direction. You must state both to fully describe them. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight. Distance (m) is how far an object has moved along its path. It is scalar. Displacement (m) is how far an object is from its starting point, and in which direction. It is vector. Example: you walk 300m east then 400m north. Distance = 700m. Displacement = 500m, in a direction you can find with a scale drawing. You can work out this straight-line distance from start to finish using Pythagoras. Speed (m/s) = distance ÷ time. It is scalar. Velocity (m/s) = displacement ÷ time. It is vector. Speed and velocity can have the same number. But velocity must always include a direction. 'A car drives at 20 m/s' gives speed. 'A car drives at 20 m/s due north' gives velocity. Higher only: an object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity. Its speed stays the same, but its direction keeps changing.
writeBullets: Scalar — magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, energy, temperature
Vector — magnitude AND direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight
Distance (m) — how far moved along the path (scalar)
Displacement (m) — straight-line distance from start with direction (vector)
Speed (m/s) — distance ÷ time, no direction needed
Velocity (m/s) — displacement ÷ time, direction must be stated

keyTerms.def: A quantity with magnitude only, no direction (e.g. speed, mass, distance)
A quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g. velocity, force, displacement)
Straight-line distance from start to current position, including direction

keyPoints.memTip: SVD — Scalars: Speed, Volume, Distance. Vectors: Velocity, Weight, Displacement.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to write 'velocity = 20 m/s' without a direction and lose the mark. Always give the direction.

keyPoints.heading: Speed, velocity and distance-time graphs
keyPoints.content: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Equation: v = d/t. Rearrangements: d = vt, t = d/v. Worked example: a cyclist travels 450m in 30s. Speed = 450 ÷ 30 = 15 m/s. Typical speeds to remember: - walking ≈ 1.5 m/s - running ≈ 3 m/s - cycling ≈ 6 m/s - car on a motorway ≈ 30 m/s - speed of sound in air ≈ 330 m/s - speed of light ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s Each type of transport has its own typical speed. A car on a motorway, at about 30 m/s, is one example. Speed is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car, their speed keeps changing. How fast a person walks, runs or cycles depends on age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary. To find a speed, measure a distance and a time, then divide the distance by the time. Measure the distance with a tape measure or a trundle wheel. Time it with a stopwatch, or with light gates for short times. Distance-time (d-t) graphs: the gradient (slope) of a d-t graph equals the speed. A horizontal line means the object is stationary (distance not changing). A straight diagonal line means constant speed (distance increasing at a steady rate). A curved line means the speed is changing. If the curve is getting steeper, the object is speeding up. If it is flattening, it is slowing down. A steeper gradient on a d-t graph always means a faster speed. Higher only: if an object is accelerating, draw a tangent to the curve at the time you want. The gradient of the tangent is the speed.
writeBullets: Average speed (m/s) = total distance (m) ÷ total time (s), equation: v = d/t
d-t graph gradient = speed — steeper means faster
Horizontal line on d-t graph — object is stationary
Straight diagonal line — constant (steady) speed
Curved line on d-t graph — changing speed (acceleration or deceleration)
Typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, motorway car 30 m/s, sound 330 m/s

keyTerms.def: Total distance divided by total time for a journey
Slope of a graph — on a d-t graph, gradient equals speed

keyPoints.memTip: Speed = Distance over Time. Triangle: put D on top, v and t on the bottom.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Gradient calculations on d-t graphs come up almost every year. Make sure you can pick two points and work out rise over run.

keyPoints.heading: Acceleration and velocity-time graphs
keyPoints.content: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Equation: a = (v − u) / t, where v = final velocity, u = initial velocity, t = time. Unit: m/s². Worked example: a car accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 10s. a = (30 − 0) ÷ 10 = 3 m/s². Deceleration is negative acceleration. The velocity is decreasing. If u = 20 m/s, v = 0, t = 4s: a = (0 − 20) ÷ 4 = −5 m/s² (negative sign means decelerating). Velocity-time (v-t) graphs: the gradient of a v-t graph equals acceleration. The area under a v-t graph equals the distance travelled. A horizontal line on a v-t graph means constant velocity (zero acceleration). An upward slope means the object is accelerating. A downward slope means it is decelerating. A curved line on a v-t graph means the acceleration itself is changing (non-uniform acceleration). For a triangle on a v-t graph: area = ½ × base × height. For a trapezium: area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height. Higher only: if the line on a v-t graph is curved, find the area by counting the squares under it. Multiply the number of squares by the distance one square stands for. Everyday accelerations are a few metres per second squared. A car speeding up from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s accelerates at 3 m/s². An object falling freely near the Earth accelerates at about 9.8 m/s².
writeBullets: Acceleration (m/s²) = change in velocity ÷ time: a = (v − u) / t
Deceleration — negative acceleration, velocity is decreasing
v-t graph gradient = acceleration — upward slope means speeding up
Horizontal line on v-t graph — constant velocity, zero acceleration
Area under v-t graph = distance (displacement) travelled
Curved v-t line — non-uniform (changing) acceleration

keyTerms.def: Rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s²; can be positive (speeding up) or negative (slowing down)
Negative acceleration — the object is slowing down

keyPoints.memTip: v-t graph: gradient = acceleration; area under the line = distance travelled.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Area under v-t graph calculations come up as 6-mark questions. Practise splitting shapes into rectangles and triangles.

keyPoints.heading: Equations of motion (SUVAT)
keyPoints.content: For uniform acceleration, one equation links velocity, acceleration and distance: v² − u² = 2 a s - v is the final velocity, in m/s - u is the initial velocity, in m/s - a is the acceleration, in m/s² - s is the distance, in m It needs no time. You can also rearrange a = (v − u) / t to give v = u + at. Worked example 1: a ball rolls from rest (u = 0) with an acceleration of 2 m/s² over 25 m. Find its final velocity. v² − u² = 2as → v² − 0 = 2 × 2 × 25 = 100 → v = √100 = 10 m/s. Worked example 2: a car brakes from 20 m/s to rest over 40 m. Find its deceleration. v² − u² = 2as → 0 − 400 = 2 × a × 40 → 80a = −400 → a = −5 m/s² (decelerating at 5 m/s²).
writeBullets: v² − u² = 2as: v final velocity (m/s), u initial velocity (m/s), a acceleration (m/s²), s distance (m)
v = u + at is a = (v − u)/t rearranged
Use v² − u² = 2as when no time is given
Square both velocities before you subtract
Watch signs: deceleration gives a negative value for a

keyTerms.def: The five motion quantities: displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time

keyPoints.memTip: v² − u² = 2as has no t in it: use it when the time is not given.
keyPoints.tutor_note: v² − u² = 2as is the equation of motion to know, and it hides time. Make sure you can spot when to use it.

keyPoints.heading: Terminal velocity and non-uniform acceleration
keyPoints.content: Uniform acceleration: the acceleration is constant. Velocity changes by the same amount each second. This gives a straight line on a v-t graph. Non-uniform acceleration: the rate of change of velocity is itself changing. This gives a curved line on a v-t graph. Free fall: ignore air resistance. Then all objects near Earth's surface fall with the same acceleration, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward. Mass does not affect the rate of free fall. Terminal velocity: as an object falls, air resistance increases with speed. At some point, air resistance equals weight. Resultant force = 0 → no more acceleration → the object falls at a constant (terminal) velocity. Skydiver story: (1) Jumps. Accelerates downward; air resistance is small. (2) As speed increases, air resistance increases. The net force and the acceleration both decrease. (3) Terminal velocity is reached (~55 m/s). Constant speed. (4) Parachute opens. Drag increases hugely, so the net force is now upward. Decelerates rapidly. (5) A new, lower terminal velocity is reached (~5 m/s). Lands safely. On a v-t graph, the skydiver's fall shows a curve that levels off at terminal velocity. Then there is a sharp drop when the parachute opens. Then it levels off again at the lower terminal velocity.
writeBullets: Uniform acceleration — constant a, straight line on v-t graph
Non-uniform acceleration — changing a, curved line on v-t graph
Free fall — all objects accelerate at g ≈ 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance)
Terminal velocity — air resistance equals weight, resultant force = 0, constant velocity
Skydiver accelerates → air resistance grows → acceleration decreases → terminal velocity
Parachute opens → massive drag → decelerates to new lower terminal velocity

keyTerms.def: Constant falling speed reached when air resistance exactly balances weight, giving zero resultant force
Falling under gravity alone with no air resistance; acceleration = g ≈ 9.8 m/s²

keyPoints.memTip: Terminal velocity: T for Terminal, T for Two forces balanced (weight = drag). No net force → no acceleration.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Describing the skydiver's v-t graph in words is a very common 4-mark question. Practise the five stages.

keyPoints.heading: Contact and non-contact forces
keyPoints.content: A force is a push or a pull on an object. It comes from the object's interaction with another object. Every force between objects is one of two kinds. - Contact forces: the objects are physically touching. Examples: friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force. - Non-contact forces: the objects are physically separated. Examples: gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force. An interaction between a pair of objects produces a force on each object. Example: a book rests on a table. The book pushes down on the table. The table pushes up on the book with a normal contact force. Another example: the Earth pulls you down, and you pull the Earth up. Both are gravitational forces. Force is a vector quantity. You can show a force as an arrow. The length of the arrow shows the size of the force. The arrow points in the direction of the force.
writeBullets: Force: a push or pull from an interaction with another object
Contact forces (objects touching): friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force
Non-contact forces (objects separated): gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic
An interaction between two objects produces a force on each object
Force is a vector: draw it as an arrow; length = size, arrow = direction

keyTerms.def: A force between objects that are physically touching, such as friction, air resistance, tension or normal contact force
A force between objects that are physically separated, such as gravitational, electrostatic or magnetic force

keyPoints.memTip: Touching = contact. Apart = non-contact: Gravity, Electrostatic, Magnetic (GEM).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask the student to name the second force in each pair. This checks they see that both objects feel a force.

tables.title: Distance-time vs velocity-time graphs — what each feature tells you

0.question: A cyclist rides at 6 m/s towards the west. Is this a speed or a velocity, and why?
options: Velocity, because it gives a size and a direction
Speed, because the direction does not change the number
Velocity, because its unit is metres per second
Speed, because it says how fast the cyclist moves
0.correctFeedback: Yes. It gives a size, 6 m/s, and a direction, west. A quantity with both is a vector, so this is a velocity.
0.wrongFeedback: It is a velocity. A velocity gives a size and a direction, and this one says west. Speed and velocity share the unit m/s, so the unit cannot tell them apart.

1.question: A car travels 240m in 8s at constant speed. What is its speed?
1.wrongFeedback: Use v = d/t. Speed = 240 ÷ 8 = 30 m/s. Don't add or subtract — it's a division.

2.question: On a velocity-time graph, what does the gradient of the line represent?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Gradient on a v-t graph = acceleration (m/s²).
2.wrongFeedback: On a v-t graph, the gradient = acceleration. It's on a d-t graph that gradient = speed.

3.question: A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² over 16 m. What is the cyclist's final velocity?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2 × 2 × 16 = 64, so v = √64 = 8 m/s.
3.wrongFeedback: Use v² = u² + 2as. From rest, u = 0, so v² = 2 × 2 × 16 = 64. Then take the square root: v = 8 m/s.

4.question: Why does a falling skydiver stop speeding up and reach terminal velocity?
options: Air resistance grows with speed until it equals the weight
The weight of the skydiver gets smaller during the fall
Gravity stops acting once the skydiver is falling fast
Air resistance becomes bigger than the weight and stays so
4.correctFeedback: Correct. Air resistance rises with speed until it equals the weight. The resultant force is then zero, so the speed stays constant.
4.wrongFeedback: Air resistance grows as the skydiver speeds up. When it equals the weight, the resultant force is zero. With no resultant force there is no acceleration, so the speed stays constant.

5.question: Which of these is a non-contact force?
5.correctFeedback: Correct. Magnetic force acts between objects that are physically separated, so it is a non-contact force.
5.wrongFeedback: Friction, tension and air resistance need the objects to touch. Magnetic force acts between separated objects, so it is non-contact.

commonMistakes: Writing velocity without a direction. Always state the direction (for example, '20 m/s northward'), or you lose the mark.
Mixing up gradient and area on v-t graphs. Gradient = acceleration, and area = distance. They are not interchangeable.
Forgetting to square the velocities in v² − u² = 2as. Square each velocity before you subtract.
Thinking deceleration is different from acceleration. It is just negative acceleration. Use a negative sign in calculations.
Saying falling objects fall at different rates. Ignoring air resistance, all objects fall at the same g ≈ 9.8 m/s², whatever their mass.
examTips: In graph questions, always draw a large, accurate triangle to work out the gradient. Use the full line, not just a small section.
For v² − u² = 2as questions, write down v, u, a and s, and mark the one you need to find.
Terminal velocity questions ask for the shape of the v-t graph AND an explanation. Describe the forces, not just the shape.
revisionCardBullets: Scalar — magnitude only (speed, distance, mass, energy)
Vector — magnitude + direction (velocity, displacement, acceleration, force, weight)
Speed v = d/t (m/s); velocity = speed with direction
d-t graph: gradient = speed; horizontal = stationary; curve = changing speed
Acceleration a = (v − u)/t, unit m/s²; deceleration is negative a
v-t graph: gradient = acceleration; area = distance; horizontal = constant velocity
Uniform acceleration: v² − u² = 2as; v = u + at is a = (v − u)/t rearranged
Square both velocities first in v² − u² = 2as
Free fall: all objects fall at g ≈ 9.8 m/s² ignoring air resistance
Terminal velocity: air resistance = weight → zero net force → constant velocity
Skydiver: accelerates → terminal velocity → parachute → decelerates → new terminal velocity
Typical speeds: walking 1.5, running 3, cycling 6, motorway car 30, sound 330 m/s, light 3×10⁸ m/s
Contact forces (touching): friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force
Non-contact forces (separated): gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic; force is a vector
